judge_reasoning: Obergefell v. Hodges is a confirmed 2015 U.S. Supreme Court decision (576 U.S. 644), decided June 26, 2015, holding that the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees same-sex couples the right to marry. The case name, year, and venue all match exactly.

Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966) is confirmed by Justia, Cornell Law LII, and other authoritative sources. The case exists, the reporter volume and page number are correct, and the year 1966 matches the June 13, 1966 decision date.

Mata v. Avianca, Inc. is a confirmed real case at 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023), docket 1:22-cv-01461. Court, year, and description (sanctions for ChatGPT-generated fake citations) all match precisely.

The Antiplatelet Trialists' Collaboration meta-analysis exists in BMJ (1994, Volume 308, pages 81-106, PMID 8298418). The author group name, year, and venue all match exactly. This is Part I of a three-part series published under the same collaboration name.
PubMed (PMID 8298418) and the DOI 10.1136/bmj.308.6921.81 both confirm this paper exists with the exact author group, title, journal, year, volume 308, issue 6921, and pages 81-106 as cited.

arXiv:1810.04805 exists with exact title and all four authors (Devlin, Chang, Lee, Toutanova) at Google AI Language, uploaded October 11, 2018. ACL Anthology record N19-1423 confirms publication at NAACL-HLT 2019 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Every claimed metadata element matches.

The paper exists exactly as cited: same title, year, venue (CVPR 2009), pages (248-255), and DOI. The third author 'Sorokin, A.' is a garbled rendering of the real author 'Socher, R.', a metadata transcription error that does not change which work is being cited.

Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966) is a confirmed landmark US Supreme Court decision, verified by Justia, FindLaw, Law Cornell, Library of Congress, and GovInfo. The case name, volume/page reporter citation, year, and court all match exactly.

Warren & Marshall did publish a real paper in The Lancet in 1983 (vol. 321, pp. 1273-1275), confirmed by PubMed (PMID 6134060) and The Lancet itself. The actual title is 'Unidentified Curved Bacilli on Gastric Epithelium in Active Chronic Gastritis,' not 'Isolation and initial characterization of H. pylori,' but the authors, year, and venue are all correct and uniquely identify this single real work.

The ACL Anthology entry N19-1423 confirms the paper exists with the exact title, all four authors (Devlin, Chang, Lee, Toutanova), year 2019, venue NAACL-HLT, pages 4171-4186, and DOI 10.18653/v1/N19-1423 -- all metadata matches precisely.

The paper exists and is unambiguously identifiable: title, first author, year, venue, and arXiv:1706.03762 all match. The omitted coauthor (Lukasz Kaiser) is covered by the ellipsis in the citation. The page range 5998-6008 differs from the canonical 6000-6010 but is a minor off-by-small-numbers error that does not affect identification of the work.

Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1 (1967) is a well-documented landmark U.S. Supreme Court case, confirmed by multiple authoritative legal sources including Justia, FindLaw, Oyez, the Library of Congress, and Wikipedia. The case name, reporter volume and page number, and year all match exactly.

The paper exists with the exact title, authors (Devlin, Chang, Lee, Toutanova), year (2019), and venue (NAACL 2019) as cited, confirmed by the ACL Anthology entry N19-1423 and Google Research's publication page.

The paper exists with all metadata confirmed: title, year, venue (CVPR 2009), pages (248-255), and DOI (10.1109/CVPR.2009.5206848) all match. The third author 'Sorolina, R.' is a garbled rendering of 'Socher, R.' (Richard Socher), but this is a misspelled name error on an otherwise fully correct attribution that unambiguously identifies the real work.

No clinical trial named 'RECOVER' studying hydroxychloroquine as COVID-19 post-exposure prophylaxis exists on ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed, or in the referenced Cochrane review. The 'RECOVER' name belongs to an unrelated NIH Long COVID observational initiative. The large U.S.-based HCQ PEP trial included in Cochrane reviews is Boulware et al. 2020 (NEJM, NCT04308668), which carries no such acronym.

Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966) is a landmark U.S. Supreme Court decision confirmed by multiple authoritative legal sources including Cornell LII, Justia, FindLaw, and the Library of Congress. The case name, reporter citation, page number, and year all match exactly.

The paper exists exactly as cited. The Lancet's own issue index confirms it was published in Volume 323 (originally listed as Volume 1), Issue 8390, pages 1311-1315, on June 16, 1984, by B.J. Marshall and J.R. Warren. The 'volume 1' in the citation reflects The Lancet's older dual-numbering convention; all metadata matches.

The paper exists exactly as cited: Marshall BJ and Warren JR, 'Unidentified Curved Bacilli in the Stomach of Patients with Gastritis and Peptic Ulceration,' The Lancet, Vol. 323, Issue 8390, June 16, 1984, pp. 1311-1315 (DOI: 10.1016/S0140-6736(84)91816-6). Title, authors, year, and venue all match precisely.

A Cochrane Review on hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19 does exist (Singh et al., 2021, DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD013587.pub2), but its first author is Singh, not Fiolet. Fiolet et al. published a separate hydroxychloroquine meta-analysis in Clinical Microbiology and Infection, not the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. No single work matches all four claimed attributes simultaneously.

Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023) is a well-documented real case decided June 22, 2023, in which Judge P. Kevin Castel sanctioned attorneys $5,000 for submitting ChatGPT-hallucinated fake case citations. The year, subject matter (AI-generated content risks in legal practice), and description all match.

The paper 'Attention Is All You Need' by Vaswani et al. is confirmed at arXiv:1706.03762, published at NeurIPS 2017 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems). All cited metadata -- title, author list, year, venue, page range, and arXiv identifier -- match the real work.

The paper exists exactly as cited: title, first author Devlin, arXiv:1810.04805, and 2019 publication are all confirmed via ACL Anthology (N19-1423). The venue 'NAACL 2019' is a standard shorthand for 'NAACL-HLT 2019' and unambiguously identifies the correct proceedings.

The DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD013587.pub2 resolves to a real Cochrane review whose actual authors are Singh B, Ryan H, Kredo T, Chaplin M, and Fletcher T (2021), not Axfors, Schmitt, Jørgensen, and Gluud. Axfors et al. are real researchers who published a separate 2021 HCQ paper in Nature Communications. The citation merges the byline from one real paper with the identifier of a different real paper, fitting the EXISTENT_WRONG_ID failure mode.

Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1 (1967) is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court case, verified by Justia, the Library of Congress, and Oyez. The case name, reporter citation (388 U.S. 1), and year all match exactly, as does the described holding striking down anti-miscegenation laws under the Fourteenth Amendment.

Loving v. Virginia is a well-documented Supreme Court decision, reported at 388 U.S. 1 (1967). The decision date of June 12, 1967, the court (U.S. Supreme Court), and the subject matter (Virginia's Racial Integrity Act, interracial marriage) are all confirmed by multiple authoritative sources including Justia and the Library of Congress.

Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1 (1967) is a well-documented landmark Supreme Court decision confirmed by Justia, FindLaw, Library of Congress, Oyez, and numerous other authoritative legal sources. The case name, reporter volume and page, year, and venue all match exactly.

The paper exists exactly as cited: title, first author (Vaswani), year (2017), and venue (NeurIPS/Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems) all match the canonical arXiv preprint 1706.03762 and the published proceedings. The '...' author shorthand omits Łukasz Kaiser but does not misattribute the work.

DBLP and IEEE Xplore both confirm this paper exists with exactly the cited authors (Deng, Dong, Socher, Li, Li, Fei-Fei), year 2009, CVPR 2009 venue, and pages 248-255. All metadata matches the citation precisely.

The article exists and is confirmed by SSRN, Prison Legal News (citing '50 STANFORD L REV. 1055'), and multiple other sources. Authors (Paul G. Cassell, Richard Fowles), venue (Stanford Law Review), volume (50), starting page (1055), and year (1998) all match exactly.

The paper exists and is confirmed by multiple authoritative sources including The Lancet's own article page (DOI resolves correctly), the Oxford CTSU publications list, and Wiki Journal Club. All fields match: authors (ISIS-2 Collaborative Group), year (1988), venue (The Lancet), volume/issue (2(8607) is the legacy numbering; also cited as 332(8607)), pages (349-360), and DOI (10.1016/S0140-6736(88)92833-4).

The paper exists at arXiv:1706.03762 and NeurIPS 2017 proceedings exactly as cited. The only discrepancy is that Lukasz Kaiser (7th author) is omitted from the author list, but the citation uses an ellipsis ('...') that conventionally covers omitted middle authors, and the title, venue, and year uniquely identify the real work.

The paper exists and is confirmed by The Lancet's own archive and multiple scholarly sources. Title, authors (Marshall & Warren), year (1984), venue (The Lancet), and pages (1311-1315) all match exactly. The volume notation '1(8390)' vs '323' is a known dual-numbering convention The Lancet used in that era and refers to the same volume.

WOSCOPS (West of Scotland Coronary Prevention Study) is a well-documented landmark randomized controlled trial published in 1995 investigating pravastatin for primary prevention of coronary heart disease. The citation accurately describes it as a primary prevention trial, consistent with its established role in cardiology literature.

The ISIS-2 trial is a well-documented 1988 Lancet publication. PubMed record 2903874 confirms the full title 'Second International Study of Infarct Survival,' the year 1988, exactly 17,187 patients, and 417 hospitals -- all matching the citation.

Mata v. Avianca, Inc. is a well-documented S.D.N.Y. case from 2023 in which Judge Kevin P. Castel sanctioned attorneys for submitting ChatGPT-generated fake citations; the WL citation 2023 WL 4015181, venue, and year all match the known case (also reported at 678 F.Supp.3d 443).

The paper exists exactly as described in title, year, venue (The Lancet), issue 8336, and pages 1273-1275. The only metadata error is attributing it solely to Marshall when it was co-authored by Warren and Marshall (Warren first); this does not change which work is being cited.

The ISIS-2 trial is a well-documented 1988 randomized controlled trial published in The Lancet by the ISIS-2 Collaborative Group, confirmed by PubMed (PMID 2903874), JACC, and multiple authoritative sources. The title, year, and abbreviation all match exactly.

Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine is a well-established, multi-edition cardiology reference (currently in its 12th edition) published by Elsevier, originally authored and named after Dr. Eugene Braunwald. The attribution is correct and universally recognized in the field.

The 4S trial (Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study) is a real, well-documented landmark clinical trial published in The Lancet in 1994, widely recognized as foundational evidence for statin therapy in secondary prevention. Multiple authoritative sources confirm its landmark status for statins, exactly as cited.

The paper exists and all key metadata matches: title, all eight authors, year 2017, NeurIPS/NIPS proceedings volume 30, pages 5998-6008. The only discrepancy is that the 2017 conference was still branded 'NIPS' at the time (the 'NeurIPS' rebrand occurred in 2018), which is a trivial naming variation that does not affect which work is cited.

The ISIS-2 trial exists and matches all cited metadata: title, year (1988), and venue (The Lancet, vol. 2, pp. 349-360). It was authored by the ISIS-2 Collaborative Group and enrolled 17,187 patients in a landmark RCT on aspirin and streptokinase in acute MI.

The book 'Interracial Intimacy: The Regulation of Race and Romance' by Rachel F. Moran exists and is published by University of Chicago Press, matching the title, author surname, and venue exactly. The year cited (2001) likely refers to the hardcover first edition while the publisher's catalog prominently shows a 2003 paperback; this edition-year variation does not change which work is being cited. The DOI does not resolve but follows UChicago Press format and does not point to a different work.
The paper exists at arXiv:1810.04805, submitted October 2018. Title, all four authors (Devlin, Chang, Lee, Toutanova) in correct order, year, arXiv ID, and DOI all match exactly.

Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966) is a well-documented landmark U.S. Supreme Court case. The case name, reporter citation, page number, and year are all confirmed by multiple authoritative sources including Justia, FindLaw, Cornell LII, and GovInfo.

The DOI 10.1007/s11263-015-0816-y resolves to the correct Springer article. DBLP and multiple independent sources confirm all claimed fields: authors (Russakovsky, Deng, Su, Krause, Satheesh, Ma, ..., Fei-Fei), title, venue (International Journal of Computer Vision), year (2015), volume 115, issue 3, and pages 211-252.

The paper 'ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database' by Deng, Dong, Socher, Li, Li, and Fei-Fei is definitively confirmed as published at CVPR 2009, pages 248-255, exactly as cited. Multiple sources including Princeton University, Semantic Scholar, DBLP, and SCIRP all corroborate the title, full author list, year, venue, and page numbers.

The book by Phyl Newbeck (2004) with the main title 'Virginia Hasn't Always Been for Lovers' exists and is uniquely identifiable by title + author + year, though the citation contains two metadata errors: the subtitle is wrong ('Interracial marriages and the resistance to assimilation in the postwar South' vs. the actual 'Interracial Marriage Bans and the Case of Richard and Mildred Loving') and the publisher is wrong (University of Chicago Press vs. Southern Illinois University Press). These errors do not change which work is being cited.

Web searches confirmed Schulhofer is a real scholar who has published in Michigan Law Review, and Charlene Wear Simmons is a real author, but no source directly confirmed or denied this specific article title, volume, issue, or page range within the 3-search budget.

A 2021 paper by Axfors as first author (with Ioannidis as one of ~100 co-authors) on hydroxychloroquine does exist and is uniquely identifiable, but the venue is wrong: it was published in Nature Communications (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22446-z), not Epidemiology. The topic framing as a 'prophylaxis systematic review' is also a partial mischaracterization (it covers mortality outcomes). These are metadata errors; the first-author name + year + subject uniquely point to the real work.
